# bstr/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)/*!
[2](https://docs.rs#2)A byte string library.
[3](https://docs.rs#3)
[4](https://docs.rs#4)Byte strings are just like standard Unicode strings with one very important
[5](https://docs.rs#5)difference: byte strings are only *conventionally* UTF-8 while Rust's standard
[6](https://docs.rs#6)Unicode strings are *guaranteed* to be valid UTF-8. The primary motivation for
[7](https://docs.rs#7)byte strings is for handling arbitrary bytes that are mostly UTF-8.
[8](https://docs.rs#8)
[9](https://docs.rs#9)# Overview
[10](https://docs.rs#10)
[11](https://docs.rs#11)This crate provides two important traits that provide string oriented methods
[12](https://docs.rs#12)on `&[u8]` and `Vec<u8>` types:
[13](https://docs.rs#13)
[14](https://docs.rs#14)* [`ByteSlice`](trait.ByteSlice.html) extends the `[u8]` type with additional
[15](https://docs.rs#15)  string oriented methods.
[16](https://docs.rs#16)* [`ByteVec`](trait.ByteVec.html) extends the `Vec<u8>` type with additional
[17](https://docs.rs#17)  string oriented methods.
[18](https://docs.rs#18)
[19](https://docs.rs#19)Additionally, this crate provides two concrete byte string types that deref to
[20](https://docs.rs#20)`[u8]` and `Vec<u8>`. These are useful for storing byte string types, and come
[21](https://docs.rs#21)with convenient `std::fmt::Debug` implementations:
[22](https://docs.rs#22)
[23](https://docs.rs#23)* [`BStr`](struct.BStr.html) is a byte string slice, analogous to `str`.
[24](https://docs.rs#24)* [`BString`](struct.BString.html) is an owned growable byte string buffer,
[25](https://docs.rs#25)  analogous to `String`.
[26](https://docs.rs#26)
[27](https://docs.rs#27)Additionally, the free function [`B`](fn.B.html) serves as a convenient short
[28](https://docs.rs#28)hand for writing byte string literals.
[29](https://docs.rs#29)
[30](https://docs.rs#30)# Quick examples
[31](https://docs.rs#31)
[32](https://docs.rs#32)Byte strings build on the existing APIs for `Vec<u8>` and `&[u8]`, with
[33](https://docs.rs#33)additional string oriented methods. Operations such as iterating over
[34](https://docs.rs#34)graphemes, searching for substrings, replacing substrings, trimming and case
[35](https://docs.rs#35)conversion are examples of things not provided on the standard library `&[u8]`
[36](https://docs.rs#36)APIs but are provided by this crate. For example, this code iterates over all
[37](https://docs.rs#37)of occurrences of a substring:
[38](https://docs.rs#38)
[39](https://docs.rs#39)```
[40](https://docs.rs#40)use bstr::ByteSlice;
[41](https://docs.rs#41)
[42](https://docs.rs#42)let s = b"foo bar foo foo quux foo";
[43](https://docs.rs#43)
[44](https://docs.rs#44)let mut matches = vec![];
[45](https://docs.rs#45)for start in s.find_iter("foo") {
[46](https://docs.rs#46)    matches.push(start);
[47](https://docs.rs#47)}
[48](https://docs.rs#48)assert_eq!(matches, [0, 8, 12, 21]);
[49](https://docs.rs#49)```
[50](https://docs.rs#50)
[51](https://docs.rs#51)Here's another example showing how to do a search and replace (and also showing
[52](https://docs.rs#52)use of the `B` function):
[53](https://docs.rs#53)
[54](https://docs.rs#54)```
[55](https://docs.rs#55)# #[cfg(feature = "alloc")] {
[56](https://docs.rs#56)use bstr::{B, ByteSlice};
[57](https://docs.rs#57)
[58](https://docs.rs#58)let old = B("foo ☃☃☃ foo foo quux foo");
[59](https://docs.rs#59)let new = old.replace("foo", "hello");
[60](https://docs.rs#60)assert_eq!(new, B("hello ☃☃☃ hello hello quux hello"));
[61](https://docs.rs#61)# }
[62](https://docs.rs#62)```
[63](https://docs.rs#63)
[64](https://docs.rs#64)And here's an example that shows case conversion, even in the presence of
[65](https://docs.rs#65)invalid UTF-8:
[66](https://docs.rs#66)
[67](https://docs.rs#67)```
[68](https://docs.rs#68)# #[cfg(all(feature = "alloc", feature = "unicode"))] {
[69](https://docs.rs#69)use bstr::{ByteSlice, ByteVec};
[70](https://docs.rs#70)
[71](https://docs.rs#71)let mut lower = Vec::from("hello β");
[72](https://docs.rs#72)lower[0] = b'\xFF';
[73](https://docs.rs#73)// lowercase β is uppercased to Β
[74](https://docs.rs#74)assert_eq!(lower.to_uppercase(), b"\xFFELLO \xCE\x92");
[75](https://docs.rs#75)# }
[76](https://docs.rs#76)```
[77](https://docs.rs#77)
[78](https://docs.rs#78)# Convenient debug representation
[79](https://docs.rs#79)
[80](https://docs.rs#80)When working with byte strings, it is often useful to be able to print them
[81](https://docs.rs#81)as if they were byte strings and not sequences of integers. While this crate
[82](https://docs.rs#82)cannot affect the `std::fmt::Debug` implementations for `[u8]` and `Vec<u8>`,
[83](https://docs.rs#83)this crate does provide the `BStr` and `BString` types which have convenient
[84](https://docs.rs#84)`std::fmt::Debug` implementations.
[85](https://docs.rs#85)
[86](https://docs.rs#86)For example, this
[87](https://docs.rs#87)
[88](https://docs.rs#88)```
[89](https://docs.rs#89)use bstr::ByteSlice;
[90](https://docs.rs#90)
[91](https://docs.rs#91)let mut bytes = Vec::from("hello β");
[92](https://docs.rs#92)bytes[0] = b'\xFF';
[93](https://docs.rs#93)
[94](https://docs.rs#94)println!("{:?}", bytes.as_bstr());
[95](https://docs.rs#95)```
[96](https://docs.rs#96)
[97](https://docs.rs#97)will output `"\xFFello β"`.
[98](https://docs.rs#98)
[99](https://docs.rs#99)This example works because the
[100](https://docs.rs#100)[`ByteSlice::as_bstr`](trait.ByteSlice.html#method.as_bstr)
[101](https://docs.rs#101)method converts any `&[u8]` to a `&BStr`.
[102](https://docs.rs#102)
[103](https://docs.rs#103)# When should I use byte strings?
[104](https://docs.rs#104)
[105](https://docs.rs#105)This library reflects my belief that UTF-8 by convention is a better trade
[106](https://docs.rs#106)off in some circumstances than guaranteed UTF-8.
[107](https://docs.rs#107)
[108](https://docs.rs#108)The first time this idea hit me was in the implementation of Rust's regex
[109](https://docs.rs#109)engine. In particular, very little of the internal implementation cares at all
[110](https://docs.rs#110)about searching valid UTF-8 encoded strings. Indeed, internally, the
[111](https://docs.rs#111)implementation converts `&str` from the API to `&[u8]` fairly quickly and
[112](https://docs.rs#112)just deals with raw bytes. UTF-8 match boundaries are then guaranteed by the
[113](https://docs.rs#113)finite state machine itself rather than any specific string type. This makes it
[114](https://docs.rs#114)possible to not only run regexes on `&str` values, but also on `&[u8]` values.
[115](https://docs.rs#115)
[116](https://docs.rs#116)Why would you ever want to run a regex on a `&[u8]` though? Well, `&[u8]` is
[117](https://docs.rs#117)the fundamental way at which one reads data from all sorts of streams, via the
[118](https://docs.rs#118)standard library's [`Read`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/io/trait.Read.html)
[119](https://docs.rs#119)trait. In particular, there is no platform independent way to determine whether
[120](https://docs.rs#120)what you're reading from is some binary file or a human readable text file.
[121](https://docs.rs#121)Therefore, if you're writing a program to search files, you probably need to
[122](https://docs.rs#122)deal with `&[u8]` directly unless you're okay with first converting it to a
[123](https://docs.rs#123)`&str` and dropping any bytes that aren't valid UTF-8. (Or otherwise determine
[124](https://docs.rs#124)the encoding---which is often impractical---and perform a transcoding step.)
[125](https://docs.rs#125)Often, the simplest and most robust way to approach this is to simply treat the
[126](https://docs.rs#126)contents of a file as if it were mostly valid UTF-8 and pass through invalid
[127](https://docs.rs#127)UTF-8 untouched. This may not be the most correct approach though!
[128](https://docs.rs#128)
[129](https://docs.rs#129)One case in particular exacerbates these issues, and that's memory mapping
[130](https://docs.rs#130)a file. When you memory map a file, that file may be gigabytes big, but all
[131](https://docs.rs#131)you get is a `&[u8]`. Converting that to a `&str` all in one go is generally
[132](https://docs.rs#132)not a good idea because of the costs associated with doing so, and also
[133](https://docs.rs#133)because it generally causes one to do two passes over the data instead of
[134](https://docs.rs#134)one, which is quite undesirable. It is of course usually possible to do it an
[135](https://docs.rs#135)incremental way by only parsing chunks at a time, but this is often complex to
[136](https://docs.rs#136)do or impractical. For example, many regex engines only accept one contiguous
[137](https://docs.rs#137)sequence of bytes at a time with no way to perform incremental matching.
[138](https://docs.rs#138)
[139](https://docs.rs#139)# `bstr` in public APIs
[140](https://docs.rs#140)
[141](https://docs.rs#141)This library is past version `1` and is expected to remain at version `1` for
[142](https://docs.rs#142)the foreseeable future. Therefore, it is encouraged to put types from `bstr`
[143](https://docs.rs#143)(like `BStr` and `BString`) in your public API if that makes sense for your
[144](https://docs.rs#144)crate.
[145](https://docs.rs#145)
[146](https://docs.rs#146)With that said, in general, it should be possible to avoid putting anything
[147](https://docs.rs#147)in this crate into your public APIs. Namely, you should never need to use the
[148](https://docs.rs#148)`ByteSlice` or `ByteVec` traits as bounds on public APIs, since their only
[149](https://docs.rs#149)purpose is to extend the methods on the concrete types `[u8]` and `Vec<u8>`,
[150](https://docs.rs#150)respectively. Similarly, it should not be necessary to put either the `BStr` or
[151](https://docs.rs#151)`BString` types into public APIs. If you want to use them internally, then they
[152](https://docs.rs#152)can be converted to/from `[u8]`/`Vec<u8>` as needed. The conversions are free.
[153](https://docs.rs#153)
[154](https://docs.rs#154)So while it shouldn't ever be 100% necessary to make `bstr` a public
[155](https://docs.rs#155)dependency, there may be cases where it is convenient to do so. This is an
[156](https://docs.rs#156)explicitly supported use case of `bstr`, and as such, major version releases
[157](https://docs.rs#157)should be exceptionally rare.
[158](https://docs.rs#158)
[159](https://docs.rs#159)
[160](https://docs.rs#160)# Differences with standard strings
[161](https://docs.rs#161)
[162](https://docs.rs#162)The primary difference between `[u8]` and `str` is that the former is
[163](https://docs.rs#163)conventionally UTF-8 while the latter is guaranteed to be UTF-8. The phrase
[164](https://docs.rs#164)"conventionally UTF-8" means that a `[u8]` may contain bytes that do not form
[165](https://docs.rs#165)a valid UTF-8 sequence, but operations defined on the type in this crate are
[166](https://docs.rs#166)generally most useful on valid UTF-8 sequences. For example, iterating over
[167](https://docs.rs#167)Unicode codepoints or grapheme clusters is an operation that is only defined
[168](https://docs.rs#168)on valid UTF-8. Therefore, when invalid UTF-8 is encountered, the Unicode
[169](https://docs.rs#169)replacement codepoint is substituted. Thus, a byte string that is not UTF-8 at
[170](https://docs.rs#170)all is of limited utility when using these crate.
[171](https://docs.rs#171)
[172](https://docs.rs#172)However, not all operations on byte strings are specifically Unicode aware. For
[173](https://docs.rs#173)example, substring search has no specific Unicode semantics ascribed to it. It
[174](https://docs.rs#174)works just as well for byte strings that are completely valid UTF-8 as for byte
[175](https://docs.rs#175)strings that contain no valid UTF-8 at all. Similarly for replacements and
[176](https://docs.rs#176)various other operations that do not need any Unicode specific tailoring.
[177](https://docs.rs#177)
[178](https://docs.rs#178)Aside from the difference in how UTF-8 is handled, the APIs between `[u8]` and
[179](https://docs.rs#179)`str` (and `Vec<u8>` and `String`) are intentionally very similar, including
[180](https://docs.rs#180)maintaining the same behavior for corner cases in things like substring
[181](https://docs.rs#181)splitting. There are, however, some differences:
[182](https://docs.rs#182)
[183](https://docs.rs#183)* Substring search is not done with `matches`, but instead, `find_iter`.
[184](https://docs.rs#184)  In general, this crate does not define any generic
[185](https://docs.rs#185)  [`Pattern`](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/str/pattern/trait.Pattern.html)
[186](https://docs.rs#186)  infrastructure, and instead prefers adding new methods for different
[187](https://docs.rs#187)  argument types. For example, `matches` can search by a `char` or a `&str`,
[188](https://docs.rs#188)  where as `find_iter` can only search by a byte string. `find_char` can be
[189](https://docs.rs#189)  used for searching by a `char`.
[190](https://docs.rs#190)* Since `SliceConcatExt` in the standard library is unstable, it is not
[191](https://docs.rs#191)  possible to reuse that to implement `join` and `concat` methods. Instead,
[192](https://docs.rs#192)  [`join`](fn.join.html) and [`concat`](fn.concat.html) are provided as free
[193](https://docs.rs#193)  functions that perform a similar task.
[194](https://docs.rs#194)* This library bundles in a few more Unicode operations, such as grapheme,
[195](https://docs.rs#195)  word and sentence iterators. More operations, such as normalization and
[196](https://docs.rs#196)  case folding, may be provided in the future.
[197](https://docs.rs#197)* Some `String`/`str` APIs will panic if a particular index was not on a valid
[198](https://docs.rs#198)  UTF-8 code unit sequence boundary. Conversely, no such checking is performed
[199](https://docs.rs#199)  in this crate, as is consistent with treating byte strings as a sequence of
[200](https://docs.rs#200)  bytes. This means callers are responsible for maintaining a UTF-8 invariant
[201](https://docs.rs#201)  if that's important.
[202](https://docs.rs#202)* Some routines provided by this crate, such as `starts_with_str`, have a
[203](https://docs.rs#203)  `_str` suffix to differentiate them from similar routines already defined
[204](https://docs.rs#204)  on the `[u8]` type. The difference is that `starts_with` requires its
[205](https://docs.rs#205)  parameter to be a `&[u8]`, where as `starts_with_str` permits its parameter
[206](https://docs.rs#206)  to by anything that implements `AsRef<[u8]>`, which is more flexible. This
[207](https://docs.rs#207)  means you can write `bytes.starts_with_str("☃")` instead of
[208](https://docs.rs#208)  `bytes.starts_with("☃".as_bytes())`.
[209](https://docs.rs#209)
[210](https://docs.rs#210)Otherwise, you should find most of the APIs between this crate and the standard
[211](https://docs.rs#211)library string APIs to be very similar, if not identical.
[212](https://docs.rs#212)
[213](https://docs.rs#213)# Handling of invalid UTF-8
[214](https://docs.rs#214)
[215](https://docs.rs#215)Since byte strings are only *conventionally* UTF-8, there is no guarantee
[216](https://docs.rs#216)that byte strings contain valid UTF-8. Indeed, it is perfectly legal for a
[217](https://docs.rs#217)byte string to contain arbitrary bytes. However, since this library defines
[218](https://docs.rs#218)a *string* type, it provides many operations specified by Unicode. These
[219](https://docs.rs#219)operations are typically only defined over codepoints, and thus have no real
[220](https://docs.rs#220)meaning on bytes that are invalid UTF-8 because they do not map to a particular
[221](https://docs.rs#221)codepoint.
[222](https://docs.rs#222)
[223](https://docs.rs#223)For this reason, whenever operations defined only on codepoints are used, this
[224](https://docs.rs#224)library will automatically convert invalid UTF-8 to the Unicode replacement
[225](https://docs.rs#225)codepoint, `U+FFFD`, which looks like this: `�`. For example, an
[226](https://docs.rs#226)[iterator over codepoints](struct.Chars.html) will yield a Unicode
[227](https://docs.rs#227)replacement codepoint whenever it comes across bytes that are not valid UTF-8:
[228](https://docs.rs#228)
[229](https://docs.rs#229)```
[230](https://docs.rs#230)use bstr::ByteSlice;
[231](https://docs.rs#231)
[232](https://docs.rs#232)let bs = b"a\xFF\xFFz";
[233](https://docs.rs#233)let chars: Vec<char> = bs.chars().collect();
[234](https://docs.rs#234)assert_eq!(vec!['a', '\u{FFFD}', '\u{FFFD}', 'z'], chars);
[235](https://docs.rs#235)```
[236](https://docs.rs#236)
[237](https://docs.rs#237)There are a few ways in which invalid bytes can be substituted with a Unicode
[238](https://docs.rs#238)replacement codepoint. One way, not used by this crate, is to replace every
[239](https://docs.rs#239)individual invalid byte with a single replacement codepoint. In contrast, the
[240](https://docs.rs#240)approach this crate uses is called the "substitution of maximal subparts," as
[241](https://docs.rs#241)specified by the Unicode Standard (Chapter 3, Section 9). (This approach is
[242](https://docs.rs#242)also used by [W3C's Encoding Standard](https://www.w3.org/TR/encoding/).) In
[243](https://docs.rs#243)this strategy, a replacement codepoint is inserted whenever a byte is found
[244](https://docs.rs#244)that cannot possibly lead to a valid UTF-8 code unit sequence. If there were
[245](https://docs.rs#245)previous bytes that represented a *prefix* of a well-formed UTF-8 code unit
[246](https://docs.rs#246)sequence, then all of those bytes (up to 3) are substituted with a single
[247](https://docs.rs#247)replacement codepoint. For example:
[248](https://docs.rs#248)
[249](https://docs.rs#249)```
[250](https://docs.rs#250)use bstr::ByteSlice;
[251](https://docs.rs#251)
[252](https://docs.rs#252)let bs = b"a\xF0\x9F\x87z";
[253](https://docs.rs#253)let chars: Vec<char> = bs.chars().collect();
[254](https://docs.rs#254)// The bytes \xF0\x9F\x87 could lead to a valid UTF-8 sequence, but 3 of them
[255](https://docs.rs#255)// on their own are invalid. Only one replacement codepoint is substituted,
[256](https://docs.rs#256)// which demonstrates the "substitution of maximal subparts" strategy.
[257](https://docs.rs#257)assert_eq!(vec!['a', '\u{FFFD}', 'z'], chars);
[258](https://docs.rs#258)```
[259](https://docs.rs#259)
[260](https://docs.rs#260)If you do need to access the raw bytes for some reason in an iterator like
[261](https://docs.rs#261)`Chars`, then you should use the iterator's "indices" variant, which gives
[262](https://docs.rs#262)the byte offsets containing the invalid UTF-8 bytes that were substituted with
[263](https://docs.rs#263)the replacement codepoint. For example:
[264](https://docs.rs#264)
[265](https://docs.rs#265)```
[266](https://docs.rs#266)use bstr::{B, ByteSlice};
[267](https://docs.rs#267)
[268](https://docs.rs#268)let bs = b"a\xE2\x98z";
[269](https://docs.rs#269)let chars: Vec<(usize, usize, char)> = bs.char_indices().collect();
[270](https://docs.rs#270)// Even though the replacement codepoint is encoded as 3 bytes itself, the
[271](https://docs.rs#271)// byte range given here is only two bytes, corresponding to the original
[272](https://docs.rs#272)// raw bytes.
[273](https://docs.rs#273)assert_eq!(vec![(0, 1, 'a'), (1, 3, '\u{FFFD}'), (3, 4, 'z')], chars);
[274](https://docs.rs#274)
[275](https://docs.rs#275)// Thus, getting the original raw bytes is as simple as slicing the original
[276](https://docs.rs#276)// byte string:
[277](https://docs.rs#277)let chars: Vec<&[u8]> = bs.char_indices().map(|(s, e, _)| &bs[s..e]).collect();
[278](https://docs.rs#278)assert_eq!(vec![B("a"), B(b"\xE2\x98"), B("z")], chars);
[279](https://docs.rs#279)```
[280](https://docs.rs#280)
[281](https://docs.rs#281)# File paths and OS strings
[282](https://docs.rs#282)
[283](https://docs.rs#283)One of the premiere features of Rust's standard library is how it handles file
[284](https://docs.rs#284)paths. In particular, it makes it very hard to write incorrect code while
[285](https://docs.rs#285)simultaneously providing a correct cross platform abstraction for manipulating
[286](https://docs.rs#286)file paths. The key challenge that one faces with file paths across platforms
[287](https://docs.rs#287)is derived from the following observations:
[288](https://docs.rs#288)
[289](https://docs.rs#289)* On most Unix-like systems, file paths are an arbitrary sequence of bytes.
[290](https://docs.rs#290)* On Windows, file paths are an arbitrary sequence of 16-bit integers.
[291](https://docs.rs#291)
[292](https://docs.rs#292)(In both cases, certain sequences aren't allowed. For example a `NUL` byte is
[293](https://docs.rs#293)not allowed in either case. But we can ignore this for the purposes of this
[294](https://docs.rs#294)section.)
[295](https://docs.rs#295)
[296](https://docs.rs#296)Byte strings, like the ones provided in this crate, line up really well with
[297](https://docs.rs#297)file paths on Unix like systems, which are themselves just arbitrary sequences
[298](https://docs.rs#298)of bytes. It turns out that if you treat them as "mostly UTF-8," then things
[299](https://docs.rs#299)work out pretty well. On the contrary, byte strings _don't_ really work
[300](https://docs.rs#300)that well on Windows because it's not possible to correctly roundtrip file
[301](https://docs.rs#301)paths between 16-bit integers and something that looks like UTF-8 _without_
[302](https://docs.rs#302)explicitly defining an encoding to do this for you, which is anathema to byte
[303](https://docs.rs#303)strings, which are just bytes.
[304](https://docs.rs#304)
[305](https://docs.rs#305)Rust's standard library elegantly solves this problem by specifying an
[306](https://docs.rs#306)internal encoding for file paths that's only used on Windows called
[307](https://docs.rs#307)[WTF-8](https://simonsapin.github.io/wtf-8/). Its key properties are that they
[308](https://docs.rs#308)permit losslessly roundtripping file paths on Windows by extending UTF-8 to
[309](https://docs.rs#309)support an encoding of surrogate codepoints, while simultaneously supporting
[310](https://docs.rs#310)zero-cost conversion from Rust's Unicode strings to file paths. (Since UTF-8 is
[311](https://docs.rs#311)a proper subset of WTF-8.)
[312](https://docs.rs#312)
[313](https://docs.rs#313)The fundamental point at which the above strategy fails is when you want to
[314](https://docs.rs#314)treat file paths as things that look like strings in a zero cost way. In most
[315](https://docs.rs#315)cases, this is actually the wrong thing to do, but some cases call for it,
[316](https://docs.rs#316)for example, glob or regex matching on file paths. This is because WTF-8 is
[317](https://docs.rs#317)treated as an internal implementation detail, and there is no way to access
[318](https://docs.rs#318)those bytes via a public API. Therefore, such consumers are limited in what
[319](https://docs.rs#319)they can do:
[320](https://docs.rs#320)
[321](https://docs.rs#321)1. One could re-implement WTF-8 and re-encode file paths on Windows to WTF-8
[322](https://docs.rs#322)   by accessing their underlying 16-bit integer representation. Unfortunately,
[323](https://docs.rs#323)   this isn't zero cost (it introduces a second WTF-8 decoding step) and it's
[324](https://docs.rs#324)   not clear this is a good thing to do, since WTF-8 should ideally remain an
[325](https://docs.rs#325)   internal implementation detail. This is roughly the approach taken by the
[326](https://docs.rs#326)   [`os_str_bytes`](https://crates.io/crates/os_str_bytes) crate.
[327](https://docs.rs#327)2. One could instead declare that they will not handle paths on Windows that
[328](https://docs.rs#328)   are not valid UTF-16, and return an error when one is encountered.
[329](https://docs.rs#329)3. Like (2), but instead of returning an error, lossily decode the file path
[330](https://docs.rs#330)   on Windows that isn't valid UTF-16 into UTF-16 by replacing invalid bytes
[331](https://docs.rs#331)   with the Unicode replacement codepoint.
[332](https://docs.rs#332)
[333](https://docs.rs#333)While this library may provide facilities for (1) in the future, currently,
[334](https://docs.rs#334)this library only provides facilities for (2) and (3). In particular, a suite
[335](https://docs.rs#335)of conversion functions are provided that permit converting between byte
[336](https://docs.rs#336)strings, OS strings and file paths. For owned byte strings, they are:
[337](https://docs.rs#337)
[338](https://docs.rs#338)* [`ByteVec::from_os_string`](trait.ByteVec.html#method.from_os_string)
[339](https://docs.rs#339)* [`ByteVec::from_os_str_lossy`](trait.ByteVec.html#method.from_os_str_lossy)
[340](https://docs.rs#340)* [`ByteVec::from_path_buf`](trait.ByteVec.html#method.from_path_buf)
[341](https://docs.rs#341)* [`ByteVec::from_path_lossy`](trait.ByteVec.html#method.from_path_lossy)
[342](https://docs.rs#342)* [`ByteVec::into_os_string`](trait.ByteVec.html#method.into_os_string)
[343](https://docs.rs#343)* [`ByteVec::into_os_string_lossy`](trait.ByteVec.html#method.into_os_string_lossy)
[344](https://docs.rs#344)* [`ByteVec::into_path_buf`](trait.ByteVec.html#method.into_path_buf)
[345](https://docs.rs#345)* [`ByteVec::into_path_buf_lossy`](trait.ByteVec.html#method.into_path_buf_lossy)
[346](https://docs.rs#346)
[347](https://docs.rs#347)For byte string slices, they are:
[348](https://docs.rs#348)
[349](https://docs.rs#349)* [`ByteSlice::from_os_str`](trait.ByteSlice.html#method.from_os_str)
[350](https://docs.rs#350)* [`ByteSlice::from_path`](trait.ByteSlice.html#method.from_path)
[351](https://docs.rs#351)* [`ByteSlice::to_os_str`](trait.ByteSlice.html#method.to_os_str)
[352](https://docs.rs#352)* [`ByteSlice::to_os_str_lossy`](trait.ByteSlice.html#method.to_os_str_lossy)
[353](https://docs.rs#353)* [`ByteSlice::to_path`](trait.ByteSlice.html#method.to_path)
[354](https://docs.rs#354)* [`ByteSlice::to_path_lossy`](trait.ByteSlice.html#method.to_path_lossy)
[355](https://docs.rs#355)
[356](https://docs.rs#356)On Unix, all of these conversions are rigorously zero cost, which gives one
[357](https://docs.rs#357)a way to ergonomically deal with raw file paths exactly as they are using
[358](https://docs.rs#358)normal string-related functions. On Windows, these conversion routines perform
[359](https://docs.rs#359)a UTF-8 check and either return an error or lossily decode the file path
[360](https://docs.rs#360)into valid UTF-8, depending on which function you use. This means that you
[361](https://docs.rs#361)cannot roundtrip all file paths on Windows correctly using these conversion
[362](https://docs.rs#362)routines. However, this may be an acceptable downside since such file paths
[363](https://docs.rs#363)are exceptionally rare. Moreover, roundtripping isn't always necessary, for
[364](https://docs.rs#364)example, if all you're doing is filtering based on file paths.
[365](https://docs.rs#365)
[366](https://docs.rs#366)The reason why using byte strings for this is potentially superior than the
[367](https://docs.rs#367)standard library's approach is that a lot of Rust code is already lossily
[368](https://docs.rs#368)converting file paths to Rust's Unicode strings, which are required to be valid
[369](https://docs.rs#369)UTF-8, and thus contain latent bugs on Unix where paths with invalid UTF-8 are
[370](https://docs.rs#370)not terribly uncommon. If you instead use byte strings, then you're guaranteed
[371](https://docs.rs#371)to write correct code for Unix, at the cost of getting a corner case wrong on
[372](https://docs.rs#372)Windows.
[373](https://docs.rs#373)
[374](https://docs.rs#374)# Cargo features
[375](https://docs.rs#375)
[376](https://docs.rs#376)This crates comes with a few features that control standard library, serde
[377](https://docs.rs#377)and Unicode support.
[378](https://docs.rs#378)
[379](https://docs.rs#379)* `std` - **Enabled** by default. This provides APIs that require the standard
[380](https://docs.rs#380)  library, such as `Vec<u8>` and `PathBuf`. Enabling this feature also enables
[381](https://docs.rs#381)  the `alloc` feature and any other relevant `std` features for dependencies.
[382](https://docs.rs#382)* `alloc` - **Enabled** by default. This provides APIs that require allocations
[383](https://docs.rs#383)  via the `alloc` crate, such as `Vec<u8>`.
[384](https://docs.rs#384)* `unicode` - **Enabled** by default. This provides APIs that require sizable
[385](https://docs.rs#385)  Unicode data compiled into the binary. This includes, but is not limited to,
[386](https://docs.rs#386)  grapheme/word/sentence segmenters. When this is disabled, basic support such
[387](https://docs.rs#387)  as UTF-8 decoding is still included. Note that currently, enabling this
[388](https://docs.rs#388)  feature also requires enabling the `std` feature. It is expected that this
[389](https://docs.rs#389)  limitation will be lifted at some point.
[390](https://docs.rs#390)* `serde` - Enables implementations of serde traits for `BStr`, and also
[391](https://docs.rs#391)  `BString` when `alloc` is enabled.
[392](https://docs.rs#392)*/

}## Expand description

A trait that extends `&[u8]` with string oriented methods.

This trait is sealed and cannot be implemented outside of `bstr`.

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

Return this byte slice as a `&BStr`.

Use `&BStr` is useful because of its `fmt::Debug` representation
and various other trait implementations (such as `PartialEq` and
`PartialOrd`). In particular, the `Debug` implementation for `BStr`
shows its bytes as a normal string. For invalid UTF-8, hex escape
sequences are used.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bstr::ByteSlice;
println!("{:?}", b"foo\xFFbar".as_bstr());
```

Return this byte slice as a `&mut BStr`.

#### fn [from_os_str](https://docs.rs#method.from_os_str)(os_str: &[OsStr](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/ffi/os_str/struct.OsStr.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<&[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]>

**crate feature**only.

`std`Create an immutable byte string from an OS string slice.

When the underlying bytes of OS strings are accessible, then this
always succeeds and is zero cost. Otherwise, this returns `None` if the
given OS string is not valid UTF-8. (For example, when the underlying
bytes are inaccessible on Windows, file paths are allowed to be a
sequence of arbitrary 16-bit integers. Not all such sequences can be
transcoded to valid UTF-8.)

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use std::ffi::OsStr;
use bstr::{B, ByteSlice};
let os_str = OsStr::new("foo");
let bs = <[u8]>::from_os_str(os_str).expect("should be valid UTF-8");
assert_eq!(bs, B("foo"));
```
Create an immutable byte string from a file path.

When the underlying bytes of paths are accessible, then this always
succeeds and is zero cost. Otherwise, this returns `None` if the given
path is not valid UTF-8. (For example, when the underlying bytes are
inaccessible on Windows, file paths are allowed to be a sequence of
arbitrary 16-bit integers. Not all such sequences can be transcoded to
valid UTF-8.)

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use std::path::Path;
use bstr::{B, ByteSlice};
let path = Path::new("foo");
let bs = <[u8]>::from_path(path).expect("should be valid UTF-8");
assert_eq!(bs, B("foo"));
```
Safely convert this byte string into a `&str` if it’s valid UTF-8.

If this byte string is not valid UTF-8, then an error is returned. The error returned indicates the first invalid byte found and the length of the error.

In cases where a lossy conversion to `&str` is acceptable, then use one
of the [ to_str_lossy](https://docs.rs/trait.ByteSlice.html#method.to_str_lossy) or

[methods.](https://docs.rs/trait.ByteSlice.html#method.to_str_lossy_into)

`to_str_lossy_into`[§](https://docs.rs#examples-4)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bstr::{B, ByteSlice, ByteVec};
let s = B("☃βツ").to_str()?;
assert_eq!("☃βツ", s);
let mut bstring = <Vec<u8>>::from("☃βツ");
bstring.push(b'\xFF');
let err = bstring.to_str().unwrap_err();
assert_eq!(8, err.valid_up_to());
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bstr/ext_slice.rs.html#308-310)#### unsafe fn [to_str_unchecked](https://docs.rs#method.to_str_unchecked)(&self) -> &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bstr/ext_slice.rs.html#308-310)

#### unsafe fn [to_str_unchecked](https://docs.rs#method.to_str_unchecked)(&self) -> &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)

Unsafely convert this byte string into a `&str`, without checking for
valid UTF-8.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

Callers *must* ensure that this byte string is valid UTF-8 before
calling this method. Converting a byte string into a `&str` that is
not valid UTF-8 is considered undefined behavior.

This routine is useful in performance sensitive contexts where the
UTF-8 validity of the byte string is already known and it is
undesirable to pay the cost of an additional UTF-8 validation check
that [ to_str](https://docs.rs/trait.ByteSlice.html#method.to_str) performs.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-5)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bstr::{B, ByteSlice};
// SAFETY: This is safe because string literals are guaranteed to be
// valid UTF-8 by the Rust compiler.
let s = unsafe { B("☃βツ").to_str_unchecked() };
assert_eq!("☃βツ", s);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bstr/ext_slice.rs.html#373-396)#### fn [to_str_lossy](https://docs.rs#method.to_str_lossy)(&self) -> [Cow](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/borrow/enum.Cow.html)<'_, [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)>

**crate feature **`alloc` only.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bstr/ext_slice.rs.html#373-396)

#### fn [to_str_lossy](https://docs.rs#method.to_str_lossy)(&self) -> [Cow](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/borrow/enum.Cow.html)<'_, [str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)>

**crate feature**only.

`alloc`Convert this byte string to a valid UTF-8 string by replacing invalid
UTF-8 bytes with the Unicode replacement codepoint (`U+FFFD`).

If the byte string is already valid UTF-8, then no copying or allocation is performed and a borrrowed string slice is returned. If the byte string is not valid UTF-8, then an owned string buffer is returned with invalid bytes replaced by the replacement codepoint.

This method uses the “substitution of maximal subparts” (Unicode
Standard, Chapter 3, Section 9) strategy for inserting the replacement
codepoint. Specifically, a replacement codepoint is inserted whenever a
byte is found that cannot possibly lead to a valid code unit sequence.
If there were previous bytes that represented a prefix of a well-formed
code unit sequence, then all of those bytes are substituted with a
single replacement codepoint. The “substitution of maximal subparts”
strategy is the same strategy used by
[W3C’s Encoding standard](https://www.w3.org/TR/encoding/).
For a more precise description of the maximal subpart strategy, see
the Unicode Standard, Chapter 3, Section 9. See also
[Public Review Issue #121](https://www.unicode.org/review/pr-121.html).

N.B. Rust’s standard library also appears to use the same strategy, but it does not appear to be an API guarantee.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-6)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use std::borrow::Cow;
use bstr::ByteSlice;
let mut bstring = <Vec<u8>>::from("☃βツ");
assert_eq!(Cow::Borrowed("☃βツ"), bstring.to_str_lossy());
// Add a byte that makes the sequence invalid.
bstring.push(b'\xFF');
assert_eq!(Cow::Borrowed("☃βツ\u{FFFD}"), bstring.to_str_lossy());
```
This demonstrates the “maximal subpart” substitution logic.

```
use bstr::{B, ByteSlice};
// \x61 is the ASCII codepoint for 'a'.
// \xF1\x80\x80 is a valid 3-byte code unit prefix.
// \xE1\x80 is a valid 2-byte code unit prefix.
// \xC2 is a valid 1-byte code unit prefix.
// \x62 is the ASCII codepoint for 'b'.
//
// In sum, each of the prefixes is replaced by a single replacement
// codepoint since none of the prefixes are properly completed. This
// is in contrast to other strategies that might insert a replacement
// codepoint for every single byte.
let bs = B(b"\x61\xF1\x80\x80\xE1\x80\xC2\x62");
assert_eq!("a\u{FFFD}\u{FFFD}\u{FFFD}b", bs.to_str_lossy());
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bstr/ext_slice.rs.html#430-454)#### fn [to_str_lossy_into](https://docs.rs#method.to_str_lossy_into)(&self, dest: &mut [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html))

**crate feature **`alloc` only.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bstr/ext_slice.rs.html#430-454)

#### fn [to_str_lossy_into](https://docs.rs#method.to_str_lossy_into)(&self, dest: &mut [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html))

**crate feature**only.

`alloc`Copy the contents of this byte string into the given owned string
buffer, while replacing invalid UTF-8 code unit sequences with the
Unicode replacement codepoint (`U+FFFD`).

This method uses the same “substitution of maximal subparts” strategy
for inserting the replacement codepoint as the
[ to_str_lossy](https://docs.rs/trait.ByteSlice.html#method.to_str_lossy) method.

This routine is useful for amortizing allocation. However, unlike
`to_str_lossy`, this routine will *always* copy the contents of this
byte string into the destination buffer, even if this byte string is
valid UTF-8.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-7)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use std::borrow::Cow;
use bstr::ByteSlice;
let mut bstring = <Vec<u8>>::from("☃βツ");
// Add a byte that makes the sequence invalid.
bstring.push(b'\xFF');
let mut dest = String::new();
bstring.to_str_lossy_into(&mut dest);
assert_eq!("☃βツ\u{FFFD}", dest);
```
Create an OS string slice from this byte string.

When OS strings can be constructed from arbitrary byte sequences, this
always succeeds and is zero cost. Otherwise, this returns a UTF-8
decoding error if this byte string is not valid UTF-8. (For example,
assuming the representation of `OsStr` is opaque on Windows, file paths
are allowed to be a sequence of arbitrary 16-bit integers. There is
no obvious mapping from an arbitrary sequence of 8-bit integers to an
arbitrary sequence of 16-bit integers. If the representation of `OsStr`
is even opened up, then this will convert any sequence of bytes to an
`OsStr` without cost.)

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-8)Examples

Basic usage:

```

assert_eq!(os_str, "foo");
```

**crate feature**only.

`std`Lossily create an OS string slice from this byte string.

When OS strings can be constructed from arbitrary byte sequences, this is zero cost and always returns a slice. Otherwise, this will perform a UTF-8 check and lossily convert this byte string into valid UTF-8 using the Unicode replacement codepoint.

Note that this can prevent the correct roundtripping of file paths when
the representation of `OsStr` is opaque.

```
Create a path slice from this byte string.

When paths can be constructed from arbitrary byte sequences, this
always succeeds and is zero cost. Otherwise, this returns a UTF-8
decoding error if this byte string is not valid UTF-8. (For example,
assuming the representation of `Path` is opaque on Windows, file paths
are allowed to be a sequence of arbitrary 16-bit integers. There is
no obvious mapping from an arbitrary sequence of 8-bit integers to an
arbitrary sequence of 16-bit integers. If the representation of `Path`
is even opened up, then this will convert any sequence of bytes to an
`Path` without cost.)

Returns the index of the first occurrence of the given needle.

The needle may be any type that can be cheaply converted into a
`&[u8]`. This includes, but is not limited to, `&str` and `&[u8]`.

Note that if you’re are searching for the same needle in many
different small haystacks, it may be faster to initialize a
[ Finder](https://docs.rs/struct.Finder.html) once, and reuse it for each search.

[§](https://docs.rs#complexity)Complexity

This routine is guaranteed to have worst case linear time complexity
with respect to both the needle and the haystack. That is, this runs
in `O(needle.len() + haystack.len())` time.

This routine is also guaranteed to have worst case constant space complexity.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-16)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bstr::ByteSlice;
let s = b"foo bar baz";
assert_eq!(Some(0), s.find("foo"));
assert_eq!(Some(4), s.find("bar"));
assert_eq!(None, s.find("quux"));
```

[§](https://docs.rs#complexity-1)Complexity

Returns the index of the first occurrence of any of the bytes in the provided set.

The `byteset` may be any type that can be cheaply converted into a
`&[u8]`. This includes, but is not limited to, `&str` and `&[u8]`, but
note that passing a `&str` which contains multibyte characters may not
behave as you expect: each byte in the `&str` is treated as an
individual member of the byte set.

Note that order is irrelevant for the `byteset` parameter, and
duplicate bytes present in its body are ignored.

[§](https://docs.rs#complexity-4)Complexity

This routine is guaranteed to have worst case linear time complexity
with respect to both the set of bytes and the haystack. That is, this
runs in `O(byteset.len() + haystack.len())` time.

This routine is also guaranteed to have worst case constant space complexity.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-24)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bstr::ByteSlice;
assert_eq!(b"foo bar baz".find_byteset(b"zr"), Some(6));
assert_eq!(b"foo baz bar".find_byteset(b"bzr"), Some(4));
assert_eq!(None, b"foo baz bar".find_byteset(b"\t\n"));
// The empty byteset never matches.
assert_eq!(None, b"abc".find_byteset(b""));
assert_eq!(None, b"".find_byteset(b""));
```

Returns an iterator over substrings of this byte string, separated by the given byte string. Each element yielded is guaranteed not to include the splitter substring.

The splitter may be any type that can be cheaply converted into a
`&[u8]`. This includes, but is not limited to, `&str` and `&[u8]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-28)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bstr::{B, ByteSlice};
let x: Vec<&[u8]> = b"Mary had a little lamb".split_str(" ").collect();
assert_eq!(x, vec![
    B("Mary"), B("had"), B("a"), B("little"), B("lamb"),
]);
let x: Vec<&[u8]> = b"".split_str("X").collect();
assert_eq!(x, vec![b""]);
let x: Vec<&[u8]> = b"lionXXtigerXleopard".split_str("X").collect();
assert_eq!(x, vec![B("lion"), B(""), B("tiger"), B("leopard")]);
let x: Vec<&[u8]> = b"lion::tiger::leopard".split_str("::").collect();
assert_eq!(x, vec![B("lion"), B("tiger"), B("leopard")]);
```
If a string contains multiple contiguous separators, you will end up with empty strings yielded by the iterator:

```
use bstr::{B, ByteSlice};
let x: Vec<&[u8]> = b"||||a||b|c".split_str("|").collect();
assert_eq!(x, vec![
    B(""), B(""), B(""), B(""), B("a"), B(""), B("b"), B("c"),
]);
let x: Vec<&[u8]> = b"(///)".split_str("/").collect();
assert_eq!(x, vec![B("("), B(""), B(""), B(")")]);
```
Separators at the start or end of a string are neighbored by empty strings.

```
use bstr::{B, ByteSlice};
let x: Vec<&[u8]> = b"010".split_str("0").collect();
assert_eq!(x, vec![B(""), B("1"), B("")]);
```
When the empty string is used as a separator, it splits every **byte**
in the byte string, along with the beginning and end of the byte
string.

```
use bstr::{B, ByteSlice};
let x: Vec<&[u8]> = b"rust".split_str("").collect();
assert_eq!(x, vec![
    B(""), B("r"), B("u"), B("s"), B("t"), B(""),
]);
// Splitting by an empty string is not UTF-8 aware. Elements yielded
// may not be valid UTF-8!
let x: Vec<&[u8]> = B("☃").split_str("").collect();
assert_eq!(x, vec![
    B(""), B(b"\xE2"), B(b"\x98"), B(b"\x83"), B(""),
]);
```
Contiguous separators, especially whitespace, can lead to possibly surprising behavior. For example, this code is correct:

```
use bstr::{B, ByteSlice};
let x: Vec<&[u8]> = b"    a  b c".split_str(" ").collect();
assert_eq!(x, vec![
    B(""), B(""), B(""), B(""), B("a"), B(""), B("b"), B("c"),
]);
```
It does *not* give you `["a", "b", "c"]`. For that behavior, use
[ fields](https://docs.rs#method.fields) instead.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bstr/ext_slice.rs.html#1326-1331)

#### fn [rsplit_str](https://docs.rs#method.rsplit_str)<'h, 's, B: ?[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) + [AsRef](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.AsRef.html)<[[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]>>(
    &'h self,
    splitter: [&'s B](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html),
) -> [SplitReverse](https://docs.rs/struct.SplitReverse.html)<'h, 's> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

Returns an iterator over substrings of this byte string, separated by the given byte string, in reverse. Each element yielded is guaranteed not to include the splitter substring.

The splitter may be any type that can be cheaply converted into a
`&[u8]`. This includes, but is not limited to, `&str` and `&[u8]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-29)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bstr::{B, ByteSlice};
let x: Vec<&[u8]> =
    b"Mary had a little lamb".rsplit_str(" ").collect();
assert_eq!(x, vec![
    B("lamb"), B("little"), B("a"), B("had"), B("Mary"),
]);
let x: Vec<&[u8]> = b"".rsplit_str("X").collect();
assert_eq!(x, vec![b""]);
let x: Vec<&[u8]> = b"lionXXtigerXleopard".rsplit_str("X").collect();
assert_eq!(x, vec![B("leopard"), B("tiger"), B(""), B("lion")]);
let x: Vec<&[u8]> = b"lion::tiger::leopard".rsplit_str("::").collect();
assert_eq!(x, vec![B("leopard"), B("tiger"), B("lion")]);
```
If a string contains multiple contiguous separators, you will end up with empty strings yielded by the iterator:

```
use bstr::{B, ByteSlice};
let x: Vec<&[u8]> = b"||||a||b|c".rsplit_str("|").collect();
assert_eq!(x, vec![
    B("c"), B("b"), B(""), B("a"), B(""), B(""), B(""), B(""),
]);
let x: Vec<&[u8]> = b"(///)".rsplit_str("/").collect();
assert_eq!(x, vec![B(")"), B(""), B(""), B("(")]);
```
Separators at the start or end of a string are neighbored by empty strings.

```
use bstr::{B, ByteSlice};
let x: Vec<&[u8]> = b"010".rsplit_str("0").collect();
assert_eq!(x, vec![B(""), B("1"), B("")]);
```
When the empty string is used as a separator, it splits every **byte**
in the byte string, along with the beginning and end of the byte
string.

```
use bstr::{B, ByteSlice};
let x: Vec<&[u8]> = b"rust".rsplit_str("").collect();
assert_eq!(x, vec![
    B(""), B("t"), B("s"), B("u"), B("r"), B(""),
]);
// Splitting by an empty string is not UTF-8 aware. Elements yielded
// may not be valid UTF-8!
let x: Vec<&[u8]> = B("☃").rsplit_str("").collect();
assert_eq!(x, vec![B(""), B(b"\x83"), B(b"\x98"), B(b"\xE2"), B("")]);
```
Contiguous separators, especially whitespace, can lead to possibly surprising behavior. For example, this code is correct:

```
use bstr::{B, ByteSlice};
let x: Vec<&[u8]> = b"    a  b c".rsplit_str(" ").collect();
assert_eq!(x, vec![
    B("c"), B("b"), B(""), B("a"), B(""), B(""), B(""), B(""),
]);
```
It does *not* give you `["a", "b", "c"]`.

Split this byte string at the first occurrence of `splitter`.

If the `splitter` is found in the byte string, returns a tuple
containing the parts of the string before and after the first occurrence
of `splitter` respectively. Otherwise, if there are no occurrences of
`splitter` in the byte string, returns `None`.

The splitter may be any type that can be cheaply converted into a
`&[u8]`. This includes, but is not limited to, `&str` and `&[u8]`.

If you need to split on the *last* instance of a delimiter instead, see
the [ ByteSlice::rsplit_once_str](https://docs.rs#method.rsplit_once_str) method .

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-30)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bstr::{B, ByteSlice};
assert_eq!(
    B("foo,bar").split_once_str(","),
    Some((B("foo"), B("bar"))),
);
assert_eq!(
    B("foo,bar,baz").split_once_str(","),
    Some((B("foo"), B("bar,baz"))),
);
assert_eq!(B("foo").split_once_str(","), None);
assert_eq!(B("foo,").split_once_str(b","), Some((B("foo"), B(""))));
assert_eq!(B(",foo").split_once_str(b","), Some((B(""), B("foo"))));
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bstr/ext_slice.rs.html#1410-1419)

Returns an iterator over the Unicode scalar values in this byte string. If invalid UTF-8 is encountered, then the Unicode replacement codepoint is yielded instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-39)Examples

Basic usage:

```

```
use bstr::ByteSlice;

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bstr/ext_slice.rs.html#1834-1836)#### fn [char_indices](https://docs.rs#method.char_indices)(&self) -> [CharIndices](https://docs.rs/struct.CharIndices.html)<'_> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bstr/ext_slice.rs.html#1834-1836)

#### fn [char_indices](https://docs.rs#method.char_indices)(&self) -> [CharIndices](https://docs.rs/struct.CharIndices.html)<'_> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

Returns an iterator over the Unicode scalar values in this byte string along with their starting and ending byte index positions. If invalid UTF-8 is encountered, then the Unicode replacement codepoint is yielded instead.

Note that this is slightly different from the `CharIndices` iterator
provided by the standard library. Aside from working on possibly
invalid UTF-8, this iterator provides both the corresponding starting
and ending byte indices of each codepoint yielded. The ending position
is necessary to slice the original byte string when invalid UTF-8 bytes
are converted into a Unicode replacement codepoint, since a single
replacement codepoint can substitute anywhere from 1 to 3 invalid bytes
(inclusive).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-40)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bstr::ByteSlice;
let bs = b"\xE2\x98\x83\xFF\xF0\x9D\x9E\x83\xE2\x98\x61";
let chars: Vec<(usize, usize, char)> = bs.char_indices().collect();
assert_eq!(chars, vec![
    (0, 3, '☃'),
    (3, 4, '\u{FFFD}'),
    (4, 8, '𝞃'),
    (8, 10, '\u{FFFD}'),
    (10, 11, 'a'),
]);
```
Codepoints can also be iterated over in reverse:

```
use bstr::ByteSlice;
let bs = b"\xE2\x98\x83\xFF\xF0\x9D\x9E\x83\xE2\x98\x61";
let chars: Vec<(usize, usize, char)> = bs
    .char_indices()
    .rev()
    .collect();
assert_eq!(chars, vec![
    (10, 11, 'a'),
    (8, 10, '\u{FFFD}'),
    (4, 8, '𝞃'),
    (3, 4, '\u{FFFD}'),
    (0, 3, '☃'),
]);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bstr/ext_slice.rs.html#1871-1873)#### fn [utf8_chunks](https://docs.rs#method.utf8_chunks)(&self) -> [Utf8Chunks](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8Chunks.html)<'_> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bstr/ext_slice.rs.html#1871-1873)

#### fn [utf8_chunks](https://docs.rs#method.utf8_chunks)(&self) -> [Utf8Chunks](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8Chunks.html)<'_> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

Iterate over chunks of valid UTF-8.

The iterator returned yields chunks of valid UTF-8 separated by invalid
UTF-8 bytes, if they exist. Invalid UTF-8 bytes are always 1-3 bytes,
which are determined via the “substitution of maximal subparts”
strategy described in the docs for the
[ ByteSlice::to_str_lossy](https://docs.rs/trait.ByteSlice.html#method.to_str_lossy)
method.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-41)Examples

This example shows how to gather all valid and invalid chunks from a byte slice:

```
use bstr::{ByteSlice, Utf8Chunk};
let bytes = b"foo\xFD\xFEbar\xFF";
let (mut valid_chunks, mut invalid_chunks) = (vec![], vec![]);
for chunk in bytes.utf8_chunks() {
    if !chunk.valid().is_empty() {
        valid_chunks.push(chunk.valid());
    }
    if !chunk.invalid().is_empty() {
        invalid_chunks.push(chunk.invalid());
    }
}
assert_eq!(valid_chunks, vec!["foo", "bar"]);
assert_eq!(invalid_chunks, vec![b"\xFD", b"\xFE", b"\xFF"]);
```

This example shows how multiple codepoints can combine to form a single grapheme cluster:

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bstr/ext_slice.rs.html#1949-1951)#### fn [grapheme_indices](https://docs.rs#method.grapheme_indices)(&self) -> [GraphemeIndices](https://docs.rs/struct.GraphemeIndices.html)<'_> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

**crate feature **`unicode` only.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bstr/ext_slice.rs.html#1949-1951)

#### fn [grapheme_indices](https://docs.rs#method.grapheme_indices)(&self) -> [GraphemeIndices](https://docs.rs/struct.GraphemeIndices.html)<'_> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

**crate feature**only.

`unicode`Returns an iterator over the grapheme clusters in this byte string along with their starting and ending byte index positions. If invalid UTF-8 is encountered, then the Unicode replacement codepoint is yielded instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-43)Examples

This example shows how to get the byte offsets of each individual grapheme cluster:

```
use bstr::ByteSlice;
let bs = "a\u{0300}\u{0316}\u{1F1FA}\u{1F1F8}".as_bytes();
let graphemes: Vec<(usize, usize, &str)> =
    bs.grapheme_indices().collect();

```
This example shows what happens when invalid UTF-8 is encountered. Note
that the offsets are valid indices into the original string, and do
not necessarily correspond to the length of the `&str` returned!

```
use bstr::{ByteSlice, ByteVec};
let mut bytes = vec![];
bytes.push_str("a\u{0300}\u{0316}");
bytes.push(b'\xFF');
bytes.push_str("\u{1F1FA}\u{1F1F8}");
let graphemes: Vec<(usize, usize, &str)> =
    bytes.grapheme_indices().collect();
assert_eq!(
    graphemes,
    vec![(0, 5, "à̖"), (5, 6, "\u{FFFD}"), (6, 14, "🇺🇸")]
);
```
Returns an iterator over the words in this byte string. If invalid UTF-8 is encountered, then the Unicode replacement codepoint is yielded instead.

This is similar to
[ words_with_breaks](https://docs.rs/trait.ByteSlice.html#method.words_with_breaks),
except it only returns elements that contain a “word” character. A word
character is defined by UTS #18 (Annex C) to be the combination of the

`Alphabetic` and `Join_Control` properties, along with the
`Decimal_Number`, `Mark` and `Connector_Punctuation` general
categories.Since words are made up of one or more codepoints, this iterator
yields `&str` elements. When invalid UTF-8 is encountered, replacement
codepoints are [substituted](https://docs.rs/index.html#handling-of-invalid-utf-8).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-44)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bstr::ByteSlice;
let bs = br#"The quick ("brown") fox can't jump 32.3 feet, right?"#;
let words: Vec<&str> = bs.words().collect();
assert_eq!(words, vec![
    "The", "quick", "brown", "fox", "can't",
    "jump", "32.3", "feet", "right",
]);
```

Returns an iterator over the sentences in this byte string.

Typically, a sentence will include its trailing punctuation and whitespace. Concatenating all elements yielded by the iterator results in the original string (modulo Unicode replacement codepoint substitutions if invalid UTF-8 is encountered).

Since sentences are made up of one or more codepoints, this iterator
yields `&str` elements. When invalid UTF-8 is encountered, replacement
codepoints are [substituted](https://docs.rs/index.html#handling-of-invalid-utf-8).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-48)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bstr::ByteSlice;

    "I want this. ",
    "Not that. ",
    "Right now.",
]);
```

An iterator over all lines in a byte string, without their terminators.

For this iterator, the only line terminators recognized are `\r\n` and
`\n`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-50)Examples

Basic usage:

```

foo
bar\r
baz
quux";

]);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bstr/ext_slice.rs.html#2231-2233)#### fn [lines_with_terminator](https://docs.rs#method.lines_with_terminator)(&self) -> [LinesWithTerminator](https://docs.rs/struct.LinesWithTerminator.html)<'_> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bstr/ext_slice.rs.html#2231-2233)

#### fn [lines_with_terminator](https://docs.rs#method.lines_with_terminator)(&self) -> [LinesWithTerminator](https://docs.rs/struct.LinesWithTerminator.html)<'_> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

An iterator over all lines in a byte string, including their terminators.

For this iterator, the only line terminator recognized is `\n`. (Since
line terminators are included, this also handles `\r\n` line endings.)

Line terminators are only included if they are present in the original byte string. For example, the last line in a byte string may not end with a line terminator.

Concatenating all elements yielded by this iterator is guaranteed to yield the original byte string.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-51)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bstr::{B, ByteSlice};
let s = b"\
foo
bar\r
baz
quux";
let lines: Vec<&[u8]> = s.lines_with_terminator().collect();
assert_eq!(lines, vec![
    B("foo\n"),
    B("\n"),
    B("bar\r\n"),
    B("baz\n"),
    B("\n"),
    B("\n"),
    B("quux"),
]);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bstr/ext_slice.rs.html#2412-2416)#### fn [to_lowercase](https://docs.rs#method.to_lowercase)(&self) -> [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bstr/ext_slice.rs.html#2412-2416)

#### fn [to_lowercase](https://docs.rs#method.to_lowercase)(&self) -> [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

**crate features**only.

`alloc` and `unicode`Returns a new `Vec<u8>` containing the lowercase equivalent of this
byte string.

In this case, lowercase is defined according to the `Lowercase` Unicode
property.

If invalid UTF-8 is seen, or if a character has no lowercase variant, then it is written to the given buffer unchanged.

Note that some characters in this byte string may expand into multiple characters when changing the case, so the number of bytes written to the given byte string may not be equivalent to the number of bytes in this byte string.

If you’d like to reuse an allocation for performance reasons, then use
[ to_lowercase_into](https://docs.rs#method.to_lowercase_into) instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-58)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bstr::{B, ByteSlice};
let s = B("HELLO Β");
assert_eq!("hello β".as_bytes(), s.to_lowercase().as_bytes());
```
Scripts without case are not changed:

```
use bstr::{B, ByteSlice};
let s = B("农历新年");
assert_eq!("农历新年".as_bytes(), s.to_lowercase().as_bytes());
```
Invalid UTF-8 remains as is:

```
use bstr::{B, ByteSlice};
let s = B(b"FOO\xFFBAR\xE2\x98BAZ");
assert_eq!(B(b"foo\xFFbar\xE2\x98baz"), s.to_lowercase().as_bytes());
```

#### fn [to_ascii_uppercase](https://docs.rs#method.to_ascii_uppercase)(&self) -> [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

**crate feature**only.

`alloc`Returns a new `Vec<u8>` containing the ASCII uppercase equivalent of
this byte string.

In this case, uppercase is only defined in ASCII letters. Namely, the
letters `a-z` are converted to `A-Z`. All other bytes remain unchanged.
In particular, the length of the byte string returned is always
equivalent to the length of this byte string.

If you’d like to reuse an allocation for performance reasons, then use
[ make_ascii_uppercase](https://docs.rs#method.make_ascii_uppercase) to perform
the conversion in place.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-64)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bstr::{B, ByteSlice};
let s = B("hello β");
assert_eq!(s.to_ascii_uppercase(), B("HELLO β"));
```
Invalid UTF-8 remains as is:

```
use bstr::{B, ByteSlice};
let s = B(b"foo\xFFbar\xE2\x98baz");
assert_eq!(s.to_ascii_uppercase(), B(b"FOO\xFFBAR\xE2\x98BAZ"));
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bstr/ext_slice.rs.html#2768-2770)#### fn [make_ascii_uppercase](https://docs.rs#method.make_ascii_uppercase)(&mut self)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bstr/ext_slice.rs.html#2768-2770)

#### fn [make_ascii_uppercase](https://docs.rs#method.make_ascii_uppercase)(&mut self)

Convert this byte string to its uppercase ASCII equivalent in place.

In this case, uppercase is only defined in ASCII letters. Namely, the
letters `a-z` are converted to `A-Z`. All other bytes remain unchanged.

If you don’t need to do the conversion in
place and instead prefer convenience, then use
[ to_ascii_uppercase](https://docs.rs#method.to_ascii_uppercase) instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-65)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bstr::{B, ByteSlice};
let mut s = <Vec<u8>>::from("hello β");

assert_eq!(s, B("HELLO β"));
```
Invalid UTF-8 remains as is:

```
use bstr::{B, ByteSlice, ByteVec};
let mut s = <Vec<u8>>::from_slice(b"foo\xFFbar\xE2\x98baz");

assert_eq!(s, B(b"FOO\xFFBAR\xE2\x98BAZ"));
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bstr/ext_slice.rs.html#2809-2811)#### fn [escape_bytes](https://docs.rs#method.escape_bytes)(&self) -> [EscapeBytes](https://docs.rs/struct.EscapeBytes.html)<'_> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bstr/ext_slice.rs.html#2809-2811)

#### fn [escape_bytes](https://docs.rs#method.escape_bytes)(&self) -> [EscapeBytes](https://docs.rs/struct.EscapeBytes.html)<'_> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

Escapes this byte string into a sequence of `char` values.

When the sequence of `char` values is concatenated into a string, the
result is always valid UTF-8. Any unprintable or invalid UTF-8 in this
byte string are escaped using using `\xNN` notation. Moreover, the
characters `\0`, `\r`, `\n`, `\t` and `\` are escaped as well.

This is useful when one wants to get a human readable view of the raw bytes that is also valid UTF-8.

The iterator returned implements the `Display` trait. So one can do
`b"foo\xFFbar".escape_bytes().to_string()` to get a `String` with its
bytes escaped.

The dual of this function is [ ByteVec::unescape_bytes](https://docs.rs/trait.ByteVec.html#method.unescape_bytes).

Note that this is similar to, but not equivalent to the `Debug`
implementation on [ BStr](https://docs.rs/struct.BStr.html) and

[. The](https://docs.rs/struct.BString.html)

`BString``Debug`
implementations also use the debug representation for all Unicode
codepoints. However, this escaping routine only escapes individual
bytes. All Unicode codepoints above `U+007F` are passed through
unchanged without any escaping.[§](https://docs.rs#examples-66)Examples

```
use bstr::{B, ByteSlice};
assert_eq!(r"foo\xFFbar", b"foo\xFFbar".escape_bytes().to_string());
assert_eq!(r"foo\nbar", b"foo\nbar".escape_bytes().to_string());
assert_eq!(r"foo\tbar", b"foo\tbar".escape_bytes().to_string());
assert_eq!(r"foo\\bar", b"foo\\bar".escape_bytes().to_string());
assert_eq!(r"foo☃bar", B("foo☃bar").escape_bytes().to_string());
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bstr/ext_slice.rs.html#2836-2838)#### fn [reverse_bytes](https://docs.rs#method.reverse_bytes)(&mut self)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bstr/ext_slice.rs.html#2836-2838)

#### fn [reverse_bytes](https://docs.rs#method.reverse_bytes)(&mut self)

Reverse the bytes in this string, in place.

This is not necessarily a well formed operation! For example, if this byte string contains valid UTF-8 that isn’t ASCII, then reversing the string will likely result in invalid UTF-8 and otherwise non-sensical content.

Note that this is equivalent to the generic `[u8]::reverse` method.
This method is provided to permit callers to explicitly differentiate
between reversing bytes, codepoints and graphemes.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-67)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bstr::ByteSlice;
let mut s = <Vec<u8>>::from("hello");
s.reverse_bytes();
assert_eq!(s, "olleh".as_bytes());
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bstr/ext_slice.rs.html#2907-2920)#### fn [reverse_chars](https://docs.rs#method.reverse_chars)(&mut self)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bstr/ext_slice.rs.html#2907-2920)

#### fn [reverse_chars](https://docs.rs#method.reverse_chars)(&mut self)

Reverse the codepoints in this string, in place.

If this byte string is valid UTF-8, then its reversal by codepoint is also guaranteed to be valid UTF-8.

This operation is equivalent to the following, but without allocating:

```
use bstr::ByteSlice;
let mut s = <Vec<u8>>::from("foo☃bar");
let mut chars: Vec<char> = s.chars().collect();
chars.reverse();
let reversed: String = chars.into_iter().collect();
assert_eq!(reversed, "rab☃oof");
```
Note that this is not necessarily a well formed operation. For example,
if this byte string contains grapheme clusters with more than one
codepoint, then those grapheme clusters will not necessarily be
preserved. If you’d like to preserve grapheme clusters, then use
[ reverse_graphemes](https://docs.rs#method.reverse_graphemes) instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-68)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bstr::ByteSlice;
let mut s = <Vec<u8>>::from("foo☃bar");
s.reverse_chars();
assert_eq!(s, "rab☃oof".as_bytes());
```
This example shows that not all reversals lead to a well formed string. For example, in this case, combining marks are used to put accents over some letters, and those accent marks must appear after the codepoints they modify.

```
use bstr::{B, ByteSlice};
let mut s = <Vec<u8>>::from("résumé");
s.reverse_chars();
assert_eq!(s, B(b"\xCC\x81emus\xCC\x81er"));
```
A word of warning: the above example relies on the fact that
`résumé` is in decomposed normal form, which means there are separate
codepoints for the accents above `e`. If it is instead in composed
normal form, then the example works:

```
use bstr::{B, ByteSlice};
let mut s = <Vec<u8>>::from("résumé");
s.reverse_chars();
assert_eq!(s, B("émusér"));
```
The point here is to be cautious and not assume that just because
`reverse_chars` works in one case, that it therefore works in all
cases.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bstr/ext_slice.rs.html#2965-2980)#### fn [reverse_graphemes](https://docs.rs#method.reverse_graphemes)(&mut self)

**crate feature **`unicode` only.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bstr/ext_slice.rs.html#2965-2980)

#### fn [reverse_graphemes](https://docs.rs#method.reverse_graphemes)(&mut self)

**crate feature**only.

`unicode`Reverse the graphemes in this string, in place.

If this byte string is valid UTF-8, then its reversal by grapheme is also guaranteed to be valid UTF-8.

This operation is equivalent to the following, but without allocating:

```
use bstr::ByteSlice;
let mut s = <Vec<u8>>::from("foo☃bar");
let mut graphemes: Vec<&str> = s.graphemes().collect();
graphemes.reverse();
let reversed = graphemes.concat();
assert_eq!(reversed, "rab☃oof");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#examples-69)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bstr::ByteSlice;
let mut s = <Vec<u8>>::from("foo☃bar");
s.reverse_graphemes();
assert_eq!(s, "rab☃oof".as_bytes());
```
This example shows how this correctly handles grapheme clusters,
unlike `reverse_chars`.

```
use bstr::ByteSlice;
let mut s = <Vec<u8>>::from("résumé");
s.reverse_graphemes();
assert_eq!(s, "émusér".as_bytes());
```
Returns true if and only if every byte in this byte string is ASCII.

ASCII is an encoding that defines 128 codepoints. A byte corresponds to
an ASCII codepoint if and only if it is in the inclusive range
`[0, 127]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-70)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bstr::{B, ByteSlice};
assert!(B("abc").is_ascii());
assert!(!B("☃βツ").is_ascii());
assert!(!B(b"\xFF").is_ascii());
```
Returns true if and only if the entire byte string is valid UTF-8.

If you need location information about where a byte string’s first
invalid UTF-8 byte is, then use the [ to_str](https://docs.rs#method.to_str) method.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-71)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bstr::{B, ByteSlice};
assert!(B("abc").is_utf8());
assert!(B("☃βツ").is_utf8());
// invalid bytes
assert!(!B(b"abc\xFF").is_utf8());
// surrogate encoding
assert!(!B(b"\xED\xA0\x80").is_utf8());
// incomplete sequence
assert!(!B(b"\xF0\x9D\x9Ca").is_utf8());
// overlong sequence
assert!(!B(b"\xF0\x82\x82\xAC").is_utf8());
```
Returns the last byte in this byte string, if it’s non-empty. If this
byte string is empty, this returns `None`.

Note that this is like the generic `[u8]::last`, except this returns
the byte by value instead of a reference to the byte.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-72)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bstr::ByteSlice;
assert_eq!(Some(b'z'), b"baz".last_byte());
assert_eq!(None, b"".last_byte());
```

`alloc`## Expand description

A trait that extends `Vec<u8>` with string oriented methods.

Note that when using the constructor methods, such as
`ByteVec::from_slice`, one should actually call them using the concrete
type. For example:

```
use bstr::{B, ByteVec};
let s = Vec::from_slice(b"abc"); // NOT ByteVec::from_slice("...")
assert_eq!(s, B("abc"));
```
This trait is sealed and cannot be implemented outside of `bstr`.

`std`Lossily create a new byte string from an OS string slice.

When the underlying bytes of OS strings are accessible, then this is zero cost and always returns a slice. Otherwise, a UTF-8 check is performed and if the given OS string is not valid UTF-8, then it is lossily decoded into valid UTF-8 (with invalid bytes replaced by the Unicode replacement codepoint).

use std::ffi::OsStr;

#### fn [from_path_lossy](https://docs.rs#method.from_path_lossy)(path: &[Path](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/path/struct.Path.html)) -> [Cow](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/borrow/enum.Cow.html)<'_, [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]>

**crate feature**only.

`std`Lossily create a new byte string from a file path.

When the underlying bytes of paths are accessible, then this is zero cost and always returns a slice. Otherwise, a UTF-8 check is performed and if the given path is not valid UTF-8, then it is lossily decoded into valid UTF-8 (with invalid bytes replaced by the Unicode replacement codepoint).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-4)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use std::path::Path;
use bstr::{B, ByteVec};
let path = Path::new("foo");
let bs = Vec::from_path_lossy(path);
assert_eq!(bs, B("foo"));
```
Unescapes the given string into its raw bytes.

This looks for the escape sequences `\xNN`, `\0`, `\r`, `\n`, `\t`
and `\` and translates them into their corresponding unescaped form.

Incomplete escape sequences or things that look like escape sequences
but are not (for example, `\i` or `\xYZ`) are passed through literally.

This is the dual of [ ByteSlice::escape_bytes](https://docs.rs/trait.ByteSlice.html#method.escape_bytes).

Note that the zero or NUL byte may be represented as either `\0` or
`\x00`. Both will be unescaped into the zero byte.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-5)Examples

This shows basic usage:

```
use bstr::{B, BString, ByteVec};
assert_eq!(
    BString::from(b"foo\xFFbar"),
    Vec::unescape_bytes(r"foo\xFFbar"),
);
assert_eq!(
    BString::from(b"foo\nbar"),
    Vec::unescape_bytes(r"foo\nbar"),
);
assert_eq!(
    BString::from(b"foo\tbar"),
    Vec::unescape_bytes(r"foo\tbar"),
);
assert_eq!(
    BString::from(b"foo\\bar"),
    Vec::unescape_bytes(r"foo\\bar"),
);
assert_eq!(
    BString::from("foo☃bar"),
    Vec::unescape_bytes(r"foo☃bar"),
);
```
This shows some examples of how incomplete or “incorrect” escape sequences get passed through literally.

```
use bstr::{B, BString, ByteVec};
// Show some incomplete escape sequences.
assert_eq!(
    BString::from(br"\"),
    Vec::unescape_bytes(r"\"),
);
assert_eq!(
    BString::from(br"\"),
    Vec::unescape_bytes(r"\\"),
);
assert_eq!(
    BString::from(br"\x"),
    Vec::unescape_bytes(r"\x"),
);
assert_eq!(
    BString::from(br"\xA"),
    Vec::unescape_bytes(r"\xA"),
);
// And now some that kind of look like escape
// sequences, but aren't.
assert_eq!(
    BString::from(br"\xZ"),
    Vec::unescape_bytes(r"\xZ"),
);
assert_eq!(
    BString::from(br"\xZZ"),
    Vec::unescape_bytes(r"\xZZ"),
);
assert_eq!(
    BString::from(br"\i"),
    Vec::unescape_bytes(r"\i"),
);
assert_eq!(
    BString::from(br"\u"),
    Vec::unescape_bytes(r"\u"),
);
assert_eq!(
    BString::from(br"\u{2603}"),
    Vec::unescape_bytes(r"\u{2603}"),
);
```
Appends the given byte to the end of this byte string.

Note that this is equivalent to the generic `Vec::push` method. This
method is provided to permit callers to explicitly differentiate
between pushing bytes, codepoints and strings.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-6)Examples

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bstr/ext_vec.rs.html#505-517)#### fn [into_string](https://docs.rs#method.into_string)(self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html), [FromUtf8Error](https://docs.rs/struct.FromUtf8Error.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/bstr/ext_vec.rs.html#505-517)

#### fn [into_string](https://docs.rs#method.into_string)(self) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html), [FromUtf8Error](https://docs.rs/struct.FromUtf8Error.html)>

Converts a `Vec<u8>` into a `String` if and only if this byte string is
valid UTF-8.

If it is not valid UTF-8, then a
[ FromUtf8Error](https://docs.rs/struct.FromUtf8Error.html)
is returned. (This error can be used to examine why UTF-8 validation
failed, or to regain the original byte string.)

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-9)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bstr::ByteVec;
let bytes = Vec::from("hello");
let string = bytes.into_string().unwrap();
assert_eq!("hello", string);
```
If this byte string is not valid UTF-8, then an error will be returned. That error can then be used to inspect the location at which invalid UTF-8 was found, or to regain the original byte string:

```
use bstr::{B, ByteVec};
let bytes = Vec::from_slice(b"foo\xFFbar");
let err = bytes.into_string().unwrap_err();
assert_eq!(err.utf8_error().valid_up_to(), 3);
assert_eq!(err.utf8_error().error_len(), Some(1));
// At no point in this example is an allocation performed.
let bytes = Vec::from(err.into_vec());
assert_eq!(bytes, B(b"foo\xFFbar"));
```

#### unsafe fn [into_string_unchecked](https://docs.rs#method.into_string_unchecked)(self) -> [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

Unsafely convert this byte string into a `String`, without checking for
valid UTF-8.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

Callers *must* ensure that this byte string is valid UTF-8 before
calling this method. Converting a byte string into a `String` that is
not valid UTF-8 is considered undefined behavior.

This routine is useful in performance sensitive contexts where the
UTF-8 validity of the byte string is already known and it is
undesirable to pay the cost of an additional UTF-8 validation check
that [ into_string](https://docs.rs#method.into_string) performs.

Removes the last byte from this `Vec<u8>` and returns it.

If this byte string is empty, then `None` is returned.

If the last codepoint in this byte string is not ASCII, then removing the last byte could make this byte string contain invalid UTF-8.

Note that this is equivalent to the generic `Vec::pop` method. This
method is provided to permit callers to explicitly differentiate
between popping bytes and codepoints.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-16)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bstr::ByteVec;
let mut s = Vec::from("foo");
assert_eq!(s.pop_byte(), Some(b'o'));
assert_eq!(s.pop_byte(), Some(b'o'));
assert_eq!(s.pop_byte(), Some(b'f'));
assert_eq!(s.pop_byte(), None);
```
Removes the last codepoint from this `Vec<u8>` and returns it.

If this byte string is empty, then `None` is returned. If the last
bytes of this byte string do not correspond to a valid UTF-8 code unit
sequence, then the Unicode replacement codepoint is yielded instead in
accordance with the
[replacement codepoint substitution policy](https://docs.rs/index.html#handling-of-invalid-utf8-8).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-17)Examples

Basic usage:

```
use bstr::ByteVec;
let mut s = Vec::from("foo");
assert_eq!(s.pop_char(), Some('o'));
assert_eq!(s.pop_char(), Some('o'));
assert_eq!(s.pop_char(), Some('f'));
assert_eq!(s.pop_char(), None);
```
This shows the replacement codepoint substitution policy. Note that
the first pop yields a replacement codepoint but actually removes two
bytes. This is in contrast with subsequent pops when encountering
`\xFF` since `\xFF` is never a valid prefix for any valid UTF-8
code unit sequence.

```
use bstr::ByteVec;
let mut s = Vec::from_slice(b"f\xFF\xFF\xFFoo\xE2\x98");
assert_eq!(s.pop_char(), Some('\u{FFFD}'));
assert_eq!(s.pop_char(), Some('o'));
assert_eq!(s.pop_char(), Some('o'));
assert_eq!(s.pop_char(), Some('\u{FFFD}'));
assert_eq!(s.pop_char(), Some('\u{FFFD}'));
assert_eq!(s.pop_char(), Some('\u{FFFD}'));
assert_eq!(s.pop_char(), Some('f'));
assert_eq!(s.pop_char(), None);
```

# BStr in bstr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bstr/1.12.3/bstr/struct.BStr.html

`pub struct BStr { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A wrapper for `&[u8]` that provides convenient string oriented trait impls.

If you need ownership or a growable byte string buffer, then use
[ BString](https://docs.rs/struct.BString.html).

Using a `&BStr` is just like using a `&[u8]`, since `BStr`
implements `Deref` to `[u8]`. So all methods available on `[u8]`
are also available on `BStr`.

[§](https://docs.rs#representation)Representation

A `&BStr` has the same representation as a `&str`. That is, a `&BStr` is
a fat pointer which consists of a pointer to some bytes and a length.

[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations-1)Trait implementations

The `BStr` type has a number of trait implementations, and in particular,
defines equality and ordinal comparisons between `&BStr`, `&str` and
`&[u8]` for convenience.

The `Debug` implementation for `BStr` shows its bytes as a normal string.
For invalid UTF-8, hex escape sequences are used.

The `Display` implementation behaves as if `BStr` were first lossily
converted to a `str`. Invalid UTF-8 bytes are substituted with the Unicode
replacement codepoint, which looks like this: �.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Directly creates a `BStr` slice from anything that can be converted
to a byte slice.

This is very similar to the [ B](https://docs.rs/fn.B.html) function, except this
returns a

`&BStr` instead of a `&[u8]`.This is a cost-free conversion.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

You can create `BStr`’s from byte arrays, byte slices or even string
slices:

```
use bstr::BStr;

Converts this slice to its ASCII upper case equivalent in-place.

ASCII letters ‘a’ to ‘z’ are mapped to ‘A’ to ‘Z’, but non-ASCII letters are unchanged.

To return a new uppercased value without modifying the existing one, use
[ to_ascii_uppercase](https://docs.rs#method.to_ascii_uppercase).

Returns a reference to an element or subslice depending on the type of index.

- If given a position, returns a reference to the element at that
position or `None`if out of bounds.
- If given a range, returns the subslice corresponding to that range,
or `None`if out of bounds.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-22)Examples

```
let v = [10, 40, 30];
assert_eq!(Some(&40), v.get(1));
assert_eq!(Some(&[10, 40][..]), v.get(0..2));
assert_eq!(None, v.get(3));
assert_eq!(None, v.get(0..4));
```

Returns a reference to an element or subslice, without doing bounds checking.

For a safe alternative see [ get](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.slice.html#method.get).

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-1)Safety

Calling this method with an out-of-bounds index is * undefined behavior*
even if the resulting reference is not used.

You can think of this like `.get(index).unwrap_unchecked()`.  It’s UB
to call `.get_unchecked(len)`, even if you immediately convert to a
pointer.  And it’s UB to call `.get_unchecked(..len + 1)`,
`.get_unchecked(..=len)`, or similar.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-24)Examples

```
let x = &[1, 2, 4];
unsafe {
    assert_eq!(x.get_unchecked(1), &2);
}
```
